usage: 따다 (literally 'pluck/win') is the default verb for earning a credential through effort; 받다 only fits the moment it is physically handed to you.
The test you sit to earn the credential; 자격증 시험을 보다 = take that exam.

Name the field first: 요리 자격증, 컴퓨터 자격증, 한식조리 자격증. The field word slots directly in front, no particle. (A driver's license, though, is just 운전면허 — 면허 already means 'license', so 운전면허 자격증 is redundant.)
to be equipped with a certificate
갖추다 = to have in place as a prepared requirement; common on résumés and job postings (자격증을 갖춘 사람).
examples: 저는 자격증이 하나 있어요.
I have one certificate.
Simplest frame: 자격증이 있다 = to have one. Use 이 because 자격증 ends in a consonant.
이직하려고 자격증을 하나 더 따고 있어요.
I'm getting one more certificate to change jobs.
이직하다 = change jobs; -으려고 marks the goal. 따고 있다 = in the process of earning.
그 회사는 토익 점수보다 자격증을 더 봐요.
That company values certificates over TOEIC scores.
Here 보다 means 'to weigh/consider' when evaluating applicants — not 'to look at' literally.
nuance: 자격증 (資格證, '資格 qualification' + '證 proof-document') is the umbrella term for any official credential certifying a skill — cooking, computing, bookkeeping, forklift operation. Korean adults collect them relentlessly to pad a résumé, so it surfaces in every career-and-self-improvement chat (스펙 쌓기 'building specs'). The dividing line you must keep straight is 자격증 vs 증명서: 자격증 proves you are *qualified to do* something, while 증명서 (證明書) is a plain proof paper like a transcript (성적 증명서) or residence certificate. The trap for English speakers is the verb: in English you 'get' or even casually 'have' a certificate, but Korean reserves 따다 ('win it through effort') for earning one — never 사다 ('buy'), which sounds like a forged document, and only 받다 at the instant of conferral. Habitual partners: 자격증을 따다, 자격증을 갖추다, 자격증 시험.

mistakes: Saying 자격증을 사다 — 사다 means 'buy', implying you purchased a fake. You *earn* it: 자격증을 따다.
Using 받다 for the whole journey of qualifying. 받다 only fits the conferral moment; the effort of qualifying is 따다.
Confusing 자격증 (proof you are *qualified*) with 증명서 (a factual proof paper like a transcript). A 성적 증명서 is not a 자격증.

usage: 듣다 ('listen') is the standard verb for *any* lecture in Korean, in person or recorded — never 읽다 or 공부하다 alone.
to pay for an online course
결제하다 = to settle payment; these courses are paid subscriptions, so 결제 (not just 사다) is the natural verb.
Top 인강 강사 are minor celebrities; 1타 강사 means the #1-ranked star instructor.
-으로 marks the means/method: 인강으로 공부하다 = study by way of online lectures.
examples: 요즘 인강 들어요.
These days I take online lectures.
Bare everyday line. 인강 + 듣다 is the fixed collocation; 요즘 sets the habitual present.
학원 안 가고 인강으로 공부해요.
Instead of going to an academy, I study with online lectures.
Shows the classic trade-off: in-person 학원 vs streamed 인강. -으로 = the method.
그 인강 배속으로 들으면 시간이 진짜 절약돼요.
If you watch that lecture at higher speed, you really save time.
배속(倍速) = playback speed; 1.5배속/2배속 is a real Korean study habit. 절약되다 = gets saved.
nuance: 인강 is a clipped blend of 인터넷 강의 (인터넷 'internet' + 강의 講義 'lecture'), so it is casual, spoken slang — fine among students and friends, but you would write 인터넷 강의 in a formal report. It means specifically a *pre-recorded, streamed* video course, the backbone of Korean exam prep and self-study. Hold the line against two near terms: 인강 is recorded and on-demand, whereas 화상 수업 / 줌 수업 is a *live* online class you join in real time, and 강의 is the neutral umbrella for any lecture. The pitfall for English speakers is the verb. Because it is video, learners instinctively reach for 보다 ('watch'), but Koreans say 인강을 듣다 ('listen to') — 듣다 is idiomatically locked to lectures regardless of the medium, exactly as you '듣다' a 수업 or 강의. Habitual partners: 인강을 듣다, 인강을 결제하다, 배속으로 듣다, 인강 강사.

mistakes: Writing 인강의 by analogy with 인터넷 강의 — the clipped form drops everything after 인강; it is just 인강.
Defaulting to 보다 because it is video. The idiom is 인강을 듣다 ('listen'), the same verb used for any lecture.
Using 인강 in a formal essay or e-mail. It is colloquial; switch to 인터넷 강의 or 온라인 강의 in writing.

usage: 받다 when *you are the student* being taught — you receive the lessons.
하다 when *you are the tutor* — a classic college part-time job. Same noun, role decided by the verb.
시키다 = make/arrange-for; parents 시키다 과외 for their kids — they neither receive nor give it.
Subject goes in front: 영어 과외, 수학 과외, 피아노 과외 — no particle between.
examples: 저는 영어 과외를 받아요.
I take private English lessons.
Student's view = 받다. Subject 영어 sits directly before 과외.
대학생 때 수학 과외를 해서 용돈을 벌었어요.
I earned pocket money tutoring math in college.
Tutor's view = 하다. 용돈 = spending money; the archetypal Korean student side job.
아이한테 과외를 시킬까 고민 중이에요.
I'm wondering whether to get my kid a tutor.
Parent's view = 시키다, with -한테 marking the child who receives it. 고민 중 = mulling it over.
nuance: 과외 (課外, '課 lesson/coursework' + '外 outside' = 'outside the regular curriculum') is private, typically one-on-one tutoring, usually at the student's home, and it sits in a clear three-way contrast you should master: 과외 is personalized and premium (one tutor, one or a few students), 학원 (學院) is a commercial academy with class-sized groups, and 인강 is a recorded video course. The word's defining grammar is that one noun takes three different verbs depending on who you are: the learner 받다 (receives) it, the tutor 하다 (does/gives) it, and the parent 시키다 (arranges) it — getting these backwards is the #1 English-speaker error, since English flattens all three into 'tutor'/'get tutoring'. Note too that 과외 is not only for children: adults take 과외 for languages, instruments, or golf. Habitual partners: 과외를 받다/하다/시키다, 영어 과외, 그룹 과외.

mistakes: Swapping 받다 and 하다. The student *receives* (과외를 받다); the tutor *does* it (과외를 하다). They are not interchangeable.
Using 받다 or 하다 when a parent sets it up. Parents 시키다 — they arrange it for the child (아이에게 과외를 시키다).
Assuming 과외 means kids only. Adults get 과외 for languages and hobbies too; it is defined by being private, not by age.

usage: 보다 is the fixed verb for sitting an exam in Korean; 시험을 보다 is the parent pattern.
치다 (or formal 치르다) = to undergo a formal exam; slightly more formal/regional than 보다.
A near-national holiday in feel: stock market opens late, planes pause for the listening test.
수능 끝나고 ('after the CSAT') is a landmark phrase marking a senior's release into freedom.
examples: 내일이 수능이에요.
Tomorrow is the CSAT.
Simple identity sentence: 수능이다 = 'it is the CSAT.' 이에요 because 수능 ends in a consonant.
조카가 올해 수능을 봐서 온 가족이 긴장했어요.
My niece sat the CSAT this year, so the whole family was on edge.
수능을 보다 + family stress — shows how nation-wide the event feels. 긴장하다 = to be tense.
수능 날에는 영어 듣기 시간에 비행기도 잠깐 멈춰요.
On CSAT day, even planes pause during the English listening section.
A true cultural fact; 듣기 = listening test. Great for sounding locally informed.
nuance: 수능 is the clipped form of 대학수학능력시험 (大學修學能力試驗, literally 'university study-ability test') — the single nationwide university-entrance exam held once a year, on a Thursday in mid-November. It is not a generic final; that is precisely the distinction English speakers must keep: 기말고사 is a school's term-end exam, 모의고사 is a practice rehearsal, but 수능 is *the* one-shot national gatekeeper, and calling any big test '수능' sounds wrong to Koreans. As a resident you will feel its weight directly — altered traffic, delayed work start times, hushed neighborhoods, and the famous flight pause during the listening section. The verb is 수능을 보다 ('sit/take'), with 치다/치르다 as a more formal alternative; never 하다, because in Korean you do not 'do' an exam, you 보다 it. Habitual partners: 수능을 보다, 수능 점수, 수능 날, 수능 끝나고.

mistakes: Saying 수능을 하다. Exams are 보다 (or 치르다), never 하다 — 하다 collocates with activities, not with sitting a test.
Treating 수능 as 'the final exam.' It is specifically the once-a-year *national* college-entrance test; a school term exam is 기말고사.
Confusing 수능 (the entrance exam itself) with 입시 (the whole admissions *process* that the 수능 is one part of).

usage: 보다 = to sit the test, treating the mock like a real exam session.
to work through a practice test
풀다 ('to solve/loosen') focuses on actually doing the problems, often alone for practice.
성적 = academic results/score; used to forecast real-exam performance and pick target schools.
Mocks are scheduled and named by month (6월/9월 모평); the month carries real predictive weight.
examples: 내일 모의고사를 봐요.
I'm taking a mock exam tomorrow.
모의고사 + 보다, the sit-it sense. Simple scheduled-future use of the present tense.
모의고사를 풀고 나서 약점을 분석했어요.
After working through the practice test, I analyzed my weak points.
풀다 = do the problems; 약점 분석 (weakness analysis) is the standard follow-up routine.
이번 모의고사가 평소보다 어렵게 나왔어요.
This mock came out harder than usual.
나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic verb for how a test 'turned out.' 평소보다 = than usual.
nuance: 모의고사 (模擬考査, '模擬 imitation/simulation' + '考査 examination' = 'a simulated exam') is a full-dress rehearsal designed to mimic the real thing, above all the 수능; the high-school version run by education offices is also called 모의평가, clipped to 모평. Students sit them repeatedly to track progress and tame exam nerves. The key boundary for learners is 모의고사 vs 중간/기말고사: a 모의고사 is an ungraded *rehearsal* that predicts performance, while 중간고사 (midterm) and 기말고사 (final) are real school exams that go on your transcript — mixing them up misstates how seriously the result counts. Two verbs split the meaning: 보다 for sitting it as an exam event, 풀다 for the act of solving the questions. The English-speaker pitfall, as with all exams, is reaching for 하다; you 보다 or 풀다 a 모의고사, never 하다 it. Habitual partners: 모의고사를 보다/풀다, 모의고사 성적, 모의고사가 어렵게 나오다.

Saying 모의고사를 하다 instead of 보다 (to sit it) or 풀다 (to solve it). Exams never take 하다.
Using 풀다 when you mean the formal exam *session*. 풀다 = solve the problems; for the act of sitting it under exam conditions use 보다.

usage: to prepare for the essay exam
준비하다 = to prepare; 논술 demands dedicated, sustained practice, not last-minute review.
Marks it as a written, open-response test as opposed to 객관식 (multiple-choice).
전형(銓衡) = an admissions screening method; 논술 전형 is one defined route into university.
쓰다 ('write') for the act of producing the essay itself during the exam.
examples: 저는 논술이 어려워요.
I find essay exams hard.
Basic 논술이 어렵다 ('the essay exam is hard'); 이/가 marks the subject of the descriptive 어렵다.
논술은 정답이 하나가 아니라서 더 까다로워요.
Essay exams are trickier because there isn't one right answer.
Captures the open-ended core of 논술. 정답이 하나가 아니다 = there's no single answer.
논술 전형으로 대학에 합격했어요.
I got into university through the essay-based track.
-으로 marks the admissions route; 합격하다 = to pass/be admitted. Shows 논술 as a real pathway.
nuance: 논술 (論述, '論 to argue/reason' + '述 to state/narrate') is a structured *argumentative essay exam* that tests logical reasoning and disciplined writing, used by Korean universities as one admissions route (논술 전형) alongside grades and the 수능. The sharp contrast learners need is 논술 vs 작문/에세이: 작문 (作文) and the loanword 에세이 mean general composition or a personal/free essay, whereas 논술 is specifically a reasoned, thesis-driven argument graded on logic and structure — so a casual diary entry is 작문, never 논술. Because there is no single correct answer, whole academies (논술 학원) exist just to coach it. Watch the verbs: you 준비하다 it (prepare), 쓰다 it (write the answer), and pass via 논술 전형 — but you would not 보다 it the way you 보다 a multiple-choice 시험, since 논술 emphasizes producing text. Habitual partners: 논술을 준비하다, 논술을 쓰다, 논술 시험, 논술 전형.

論述 = 論 to argue/reason + 述 to state/narrate.
Watch the verbs: you 준비하다 it (prepare), 쓰다 it (write the answer), and pass via 논술 전형 — but you would not 보다 it the way you 보다 a multiple-choice 시험, since 논술 emphasizes producing text.

mistakes: Confusing 논술 (a reasoned argumentative exam) with 작문/에세이 (general or personal composition). Logic and structure define 논술.
Calling any writing assignment 논술. It means specifically a structured, argument-based exam, not free writing or a report (보고서).
Reaching for 하다: 논술을 하다 is off. Use 논술을 준비하다 (prepare) or 논술을 쓰다 (write the essay).

usage: 받다 = to be conferred — the formal moment the university grants it to you.
따다 ('win/pluck') foregrounds the years of effort behind obtaining it; warmer, more colloquial than 받다.
Hierarchy: 학사(學士) bachelor's, 석사(碩士) master's, 박사(博士) doctorate — each + 학위.
과정(課程) = course/program of study; 석사 학위 과정 = a master's program.
examples: 저는 학사 학위가 있어요.
I have a bachelor's degree.
학위가 있다 = to hold a degree. 학사 = bachelor's; the level word sits before 학위.
한국에서 석사 학위를 따려고 유학 왔어요.
I came to Korea to earn a master's.
유학 오다 = come abroad to study; -으려고 marks the purpose. 따다 stresses the effort.
그 자리는 관련 학위가 있어야 지원할 수 있어요.
You need a relevant degree to apply for that position.
-아야 = the requirement 'must have'; practical for job-hunting talk. 지원하다 = to apply.
nuance: 학위 (學位, '學 learning' + '位 rank/position' = 'a rank in learning') is your formal academic degree: 학사 (bachelor's), 석사 (master's), or 박사 (doctorate). The contrast you must not blur is 학위 vs 학력: 학위 is a specific *degree title* you were granted, while 학력 (學歷) is your overall *level of schooling completed* (e.g. 고졸 'high-school graduate', 대졸 'college graduate') — a job form asking 학력 wants your education level, not a degree certificate. Two verbs serve it with a nuance gap: 받다 marks the conferral ('the degree was awarded to me'), 따다 foregrounds the grind of earning it; pick by which you want to stress. Pair it with 과정 to talk about the program itself (학위 과정). In Korea 학위 matters for both employment and certain visa categories, so it is genuinely practical for residents. The English-speaker pitfall is the all-purpose 하다: you 받다 or 따다 a degree, never 학위를 하다. Habitual partners: 학위를 받다/따다, 석사 학위, 학위 과정.

Two verbs serve it with a nuance gap: 받다 marks the conferral ('the degree was awarded to me'), 따다 foregrounds the grind of earning it; pick by which you want to stress. Pair it with 과정 to talk about the program itself (학위 과정).

mistakes: Confusing 학위 (a degree title like 석사) with 학력 (overall education level like 고졸/대졸). Forms asking 학력 want the level, not the degree.
Saying 학위를 하다. A degree is received (받다) or earned (따다); 하다 does not collocate with 학위.
Treating 받다 and 따다 as identical. 받다 = the conferral moment; 따다 = the effortful achievement. Choose by emphasis.

usage: 준비하다 over a multi-year span — 입시 is a process, not a single test day.
to go through the admissions process
치르다 = to undergo a formal ordeal/exam; the right verb for living through the whole 입시.
By far the most common collocation; 대학 입시 = the university-entrance race specifically.
경쟁(競爭) = competition; 입시 is almost inseparable from 치열한 경쟁 (fierce competition).
examples: 한국 입시는 정말 치열해요.
Korean college admissions are really cutthroat.
치열하다 = fierce/cutthroat, the defining adjective for 입시. Simple descriptive sentence.
입시 때문에 고등학생들이 스트레스를 많이 받아요.
High schoolers get a lot of stress because of admissions.
때문에 = because of; 스트레스를 받다 (not 가지다) = to get stressed. A go-to social-commentary line.
요즘은 입시 제도가 자주 바뀌어서 학부모들이 헷갈려해요.
These days the admissions system changes so often that parents get confused.
제도 = system; 헷갈려하다 = to find confusing. Reflects a real, recurring Korean complaint.
nuance: 입시 (入試, '入 to enter' + '試 examination' = a clip of 입학시험 'entrance exam') refers to the *entire* entrance-examination and admissions enterprise — application strategy, the 수능, 논술, interviews, the whole multi-year campaign — not one exam. This is the precise trap for English speakers: 입시 is the umbrella *process*, whereas 수능 is a single test that happens to sit inside it, and 입학 (入學) is the actual act of *enrolling* once you are admitted; conflating 입시 with 수능 misses that the word names the entire race. It carries heavy cultural freight of brutal competition and is a perennial topic in Korean news and family life (사교육 'private education', 입시 지옥 'admissions hell'). Distinguish it also from 취업 (就業 'getting a job'): 입시 is entering *school*, 취업 is entering the *workforce*. Habitual partners: 대학 입시, 입시 준비, 입시 학원, 입시 경쟁, 입시 제도.

mistakes: Equating 입시 with a single test. It is the whole admissions process — the 수능, 논술, interviews and applications all fall under 입시.
Confusing 입시 (the entrance/admissions process) with 입학 (actually enrolling) or 취업 (entering the workforce). Different stages entirely.
Saying 스트레스를 가지다 in these sentences. Korean idiom is 스트레스를 받다 — you 'receive' stress, you don't 'have' it.

usage: 부르다 = to call out (names); what the teacher does at the start of class to check who is present.
출석 체크 is the everyday phrase; 체크하다 = to check off the present students.
인정(認定) = to recognize/grant; a sick day or official absence still 'counted' as 출석.
-률(率) turns it into a rate/percentage: 출석률이 높다 = the attendance rate is high.
examples: 출석을 불러요.
(The teacher) is calling the roll.
Core collocation 출석을 부르다. The act that opens many Korean classes.
교수님이 매 수업마다 출석을 불러요.
The professor calls roll every single class.
매 수업마다 = every class without exception; -마다 = each/every. Shows how attendance is policed.
출석만 잘 채워도 학점이 올라가요.
Just by completing attendance you can raise your grade.
채우다 = to fill/meet a quota; 학점 = course credit/grade. Reflects attendance counting toward marks.
nuance: 출석 (出席, '出 to go out/appear' + '席 seat' = 'to take one's seat') is the noun for being present, the base of everyday phrases like 출석 체크 and 출석을 부르다. In Korean universities and academies, 출석 frequently feeds directly into your grade, so it is a genuinely practical word; its antonym is 결석 (缺席 'absence'). Two distinctions trip English speakers. First, register-of-place: 출석 is showing up to *class*, 출근 (出勤) is showing up to *work*, and 참석 (參席) is attending an *event/meeting* — so you 출근하다 to the office but 참석하다 a wedding, and using 출석 for either sounds school-bound. Second, 출석 as a verb (출석하다) means 'be present at class/roll call,' so do not stretch it to events; for a ceremony or meeting say 참석하다. Habitual partners: 출석을 부르다, 출석 체크, 출석률, 출석을 인정하다.

mistakes: Using 출석 for showing up to work. That is 출근(하다); 출석 is specifically class attendance.
Saying 출석하다 for attending an event or meeting. For ceremonies and meetings use 참석하다 (to attend/participate).
Confusing 출석 (present) with 결석 (absent). They are opposites — 무단 결석 = an unexcused absence, the thing 출석 prevents.

usage: The whole word is a noun; 하다 turns it into the action 'to do cramming.'
-로 marks cramming as the *method*: study by way of last-minute effort.
to take an exam having crammed
-로 again marks the means; describes facing a test on cram-only prep.
밤새(다) = stay up all night; the prototypical 벼락치기 scenario.
examples: 저는 벼락치기를 자주 해요.
I cram a lot.
Bare frame with 하다. 자주 = often; a rueful self-description many students relate to.
벼락치기로는 좋은 점수를 받기 힘들어요.
It's hard to get a good score by cramming.
-로는 = 'by means of, as for'; 받기 힘들다 = hard to get. Standard cautionary advice.
시험이 내일인데 또 벼락치기야.
The exam's tomorrow and it's cramming again.
Casual -야 ending (반말); 또 = yet again. A relatable, self-deprecating student grumble.
nuance: 벼락치기 is a vivid native (non-Sino) compound: 벼락 ('a bolt of lightning') + 치기 (the noun form of 치다 'to strike') — literally 'striking like lightning,' i.e. frantic, all-at-once last-minute studying right before a test. It is colloquial and self-aware; students and recent grads use it about themselves with a wry, slightly guilty tone, so keep it out of academic writing — in a formal context you would rephrase it neutrally, e.g. 단기간에 몰아서 공부하다 ('study intensively in a short period'). The natural contrast is with 꾸준히 공부하다 (studying steadily over time): 벼락치기 is the short, panicked burst, the opposite of sustained effort. Two grammar points carry the English-speaker pitfalls: because it *names an activity*, it takes 하다 (벼락치기를 하다), never 보다 — you don't 'see' cramming — and to mark it as your study *method* you attach -로 (벼락치기로 공부하다). Habitual partners: 벼락치기를 하다, 벼락치기로 공부하다, 밤새 벼락치기, 시험 전날 벼락치기.

mistakes: Saying 벼락치기를 보다. Cramming is an activity you *do*: 벼락치기를 하다. 보다 (see/take-exam) does not fit.
Using it in formal or academic writing. 벼락치기 is colloquial and self-deprecating; rephrase to something neutral in essays.
Marking the method with the wrong particle. 'Study by cramming' is 벼락치기로 공부하다 (-로 = means), not 벼락치기에 or 벼락치기를 공부하다.

usage: Go-to phrase for finicky, hard-to-crack exam questions; not just hard, but fiddly.
ㅂ-irregular before a noun: 까다롭 + 은 → 까다로운, never 까다롭은.
Used for hard-to-meet requirements — scholarships, visas, applications.
입맛(taste) + 까다롭다 = fussy about food; a very common collocation about people.
examples: 이 문제 좀 까다로워요.
This question is a bit tricky.
Plain present 까다로워요 shows the ㅂ-irregular (-롭다 → -로워요). 좀 softens it.
그 교수님은 채점이 까다로워서 학점 받기 어려워요.
That professor grades strictly, so it's hard to score well.
채점(grading) + 까다롭다 is natural. -아서 links cause→result. Past would be 까다로웠어요.
장학금 신청 조건이 생각보다 까다로워요.
The scholarship requirements are pickier than I expected.
조건이 까다롭다 = fussy conditions; 생각보다 = more than expected. Practical for residents seeking aid.
nuance: 까다롭다 describes something *tricky and hard to satisfy* — fiddly exam questions, fussy requirements, or a finicky, hard-to-please person. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the final ㅂ turns to 우 before a vowel, giving 까다로워요 (present), 까다로웠어요 (past), and 까다로운 (before a noun) — memorize these because regularizing to 까다롭아요 is the single most common learner error. The crucial meaning contrast is 까다롭다 vs 어렵다: 어렵다 is plainly 'difficult/hard' in a neutral way, but 까다롭다 adds a layer of *finickiness* — picky, particular, full of fiddly conditions. So a math problem can be 어렵다 (just hard) or 까다롭다 (sneaky, full of traps); a person who is 까다롭다 is hard to please, which 어렵다 can't convey. Applied to people it leans negative (demanding, fussy), so use care describing someone's character. Habitual partners: 문제가 까다롭다, 조건이 까다롭다, 입맛이 까다롭다, 까다로운 교수님.

Using it as a plain synonym for 'difficult.' 어렵다 = simply hard; 까다롭다 adds finicky/picky/fiddly nuance, especially for conditions and people.
Casually calling a person 까다로워요 to their face. Of people it means 'fussy/hard to please' and can sound critical; soften or rephrase.

usage: The single most common pairing in a study context — keep at it day after day.
For languages, instruments, sports; emphasizes regular repetition over time.
Praises sustained persistence rather than one big push.
늘다 = to grow/improve; 꾸준히 늘다 = get better bit by bit, continuously.
examples: 매일 꾸준히 해요.
I do it steadily every day.
꾸준히 + 하다, the most generic form of encouragement to keep going. 매일 reinforces the regularity.
벼락치기보다 꾸준히 공부하는 게 나아요.
Studying steadily beats cramming.
Direct contrast with 벼락치기. -보다 = than; -는 게 낫다 = it's better to. The classic study moral.
한국어를 꾸준히 하면 금방 늘어요.
If you keep at Korean consistently, you'll improve fast.
-면 = if/when; 금방 = quickly; 늘다 = improve. Encouragement aimed straight at the learner.
nuance: 꾸준히 means doing something *steadily and consistently over time, without quitting* — it is the warm praise-word Koreans reach for to describe sustainable, unglamorous, day-after-day effort. The contrast you must internalize is 꾸준히 vs 열심히: 열심히 means 'hard, with intensity/diligence' and can describe a single burst (오늘 열심히 공부했어요 = I studied hard today), whereas 꾸준히 is inherently about *continuity* across time — you cannot be 꾸준히 for one day, because the word means you kept it up. So an all-nighter is 열심히, never 꾸준히; daily practice for a year is 꾸준히. In a self-improvement context it is the natural opposite of cramming (벼락치기) or giving up. The grammar pitfall for English speakers is part of speech: 꾸준히 is an *adverb* that modifies verbs (꾸준히 공부하다), so you cannot use it to describe a noun directly — for that you need the adjective 꾸준하다 (e.g. 꾸준한 노력 'steady effort'). Habitual partners: 꾸준히 공부하다, 꾸준히 연습하다, 꾸준히 노력하다, 꾸준히 늘다.

Pairing it with one-off actions. 꾸준히 implies repetition over time, so 'I studied 꾸준히 last night' is contradictory — that's 열심히.
